The Emperor red snapper Lutjanus sebae is a large-bodied lutjanid that inhabits coral reef and rocky substrate environments throughout the Indo-Pacific region. Field surveys and captive rearing studies have provided detailed life-history data for this commercially important species. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 28 °C [T = 28 °C], researchers have documented a maximum lifespan of 8030 days [am = 8030 days], equivalent to approximately 22 years. This extended longevity is consistent with the slow-growth, late-maturing strategy observed among many large lutjanids. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) measured during the peak spawning season reached 14% [GSI = 14%] at a water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C].

As with many iteroparous reef fishes, females of Lutjanus sebae attain sexual maturity at a fork length of 54.2 centimeters [Lp = 54.2 centimeters], a size that is typically reached after several years of growth in the wild. This length at puberty is an important management benchmark, as it corresponds to the size at which individuals begin contributing to the reproductive population. Juveniles and sub-adults below this threshold are excluded from spawning aggregations and thus do not yet contribute to recruitment. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that this pubertal length is intermediate within the genus, falling between the earlier-maturing Lutjanus johnii and the later-maturing Lutjanus argentimaculatus. The onset of vitellogenesis and spermiation in females and males respectively occurs during the austral summer months, when water temperatures and photoperiod cues align to trigger the HPG axis activation that initiates the spawning cycle.

The ultimate fork length attained by fully grown adults of this species has been recorded at 116 centimeters [Li = 116 centimeters], representing the maximum size these fish achieve under natural conditions. This asymptotic length is among the largest documented for the Lutjanus genus and places the Emperor red snapper in the upper size range of Indo-Pacific lutjanids. The growth trajectory leading to this terminal size is characterized by rapid early development during the first few years, followed by a pronounced deceleration as individuals approach their maximum length. Large adults exceeding 100 centimeters in fork length are typically older than 15 years and are predominantly females, as the species exhibits slight sexual dimorphism in ultimate size. The ecological significance of this large body size includes reduced vulnerability to gape-limited predators and the capacity to exploit a broader range of prey items, including cephalopods and smaller teleosts.

At the opposite end of the size spectrum, the wet weight at birth for Lutjanus sebae has been estimated at 0.00032 grams [Wwb = 0.00032 grams], based on the egg diameter of a closely related congener. This minuscule neonatal mass reflects the pelagic egg strategy typical of lutjanids, wherein females release large numbers of small, transparent eggs that undergo external fertilisation during broadcast spawning events. Following eclosion, the yolk-sac larvae depend entirely on their endogenous yolk reserves during the first few days post-hatching. The transition to exogenous feeding occurs once the yolk-sac is resorbed and the mouth gape has opened sufficiently to capture small zooplanktonic prey. Mortalities during this early larval period are extremely high, a demographic reality that is compensated for by the production of enormous numbers of offspring per spawning event. The selective pressures acting on this early life stage are a major determinant of year-class strength and subsequent recruitment into the adult population.

The ultimate wet weight attained by mature adults in this species reaches 32700 grams [Wwi = 32700 grams], a figure that underscores the substantial biomass that these fish can achieve over their long lifespans. This adult body mass places the species among the heaviest of the shallow-water lutjanids. The 0.00032 gram wet weight at birth and the 32700 gram adult mass reveal a dramatic increase of roughly eight orders of magnitude over the course of an individual's lifetime, an enormous scope for growth that is characteristic of tropical reef fishes combining indeterminate growth with extended longevity. The energetic demands of supporting this massive adult body are met through a diet that shifts from planktonic invertebrates in the juvenile stage to demersal fish and crustaceans in adulthood. The high ultimate wet weight also has implications for fisheries management, as the removal of very large individuals can disproportionately affect the spawning potential of the population.
